7. The learned Advocate for the appellant first of all placed before me the FIR, the charge, the evidences, the 342 statement of the accused together with the impugned judgment and other materials on record and then seriously assailed the impugned conviction and sentence of the appellant on various grounds, Firstly, the learned Advocate Mr. Faruque contended that there was substantial and purposeful delay in lodging the FIR in this case without any reasonable explanation by the prosecution and that created much doubt about the truth of the prosecution. From the records he pointed out that according to the prosecution case the alleged occurrence had taken place on 13.10.91 but the FIR was lodged by PW 1 only on 22.1.92 after about 3 months and in the FIR not a single word was expressed by the informant as to the cause of such delay in lodging the same and hence such unexplained inordinate delay casts doubt on the prosecution story. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the appellant relied upon a decision in the case of S Mohsin Sharif Vs. State reported in 7 DLR 186 and also relied on another decision in the case of Azizur Rahman and others Vs. State reported in 1984 BCR (AD) 370. 

 9. The next point argued by the learned Advocate for the appellant was, that in making the search of the appellant's house for recovery of the incriminating articles, the necessary provisions of law under section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not complied with. The learned Advocate contended that as per provisions of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, before making any search, the Officer or any other persons about to make it, shall call upon two or more respectable inhabitants of the locality of the place where the search is to be conducted to attend and witness the search, but in the instant case, the Inspector cm along with his force already entered into the house of the accused appellant and made some sort of search without calling for any local witness and then brought PW 2, the land lord of the house, only to sign the so-called seizure-list. Hence, it is the grievance of the learned advocate for the appellant that the search was not held in accordance with law in this case and the alleged recovery of heroin from the possession of the accused was false and a concoction. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the appellant relied on some decisions, one in the case of Panchu alias Paigam Ali Vs. State reported in 26 DLR 297 and another in the case of Daud Ali Vs. State reported in 27 DLR 155. 

 11. Mr. Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate, thereafter argued that in the instant case, some of the material witnesses have not been produced in court without any explanation by the prosecution. He has pointed out that the Investigating Officer of this case Md. Awlad Hossain Khan who was shown as a charge-sheet witness, the Assistant Chemical Examiner, CID, Dhaka one Abdul Awal who chemically examined the seized incriminating powder and gave his report opining that the same contained heroin have not been examined in this case. Then again some other charge-sheet witnesses No. 5, Sub-Inspector, Abul Hashem and charge-sheet witness No. 6 Sub-Inspector Faruq Bepari who allegedly recorded and filled up the FIR form have also not been produced in court in this case. The learned advocate for the appellant further pointed out that the incriminating articles i.e. the powder allegedly containing heroin as well as the other articles allegedly seized and recovered from the house of the accused appellant, have also not been marked as any material exhibit in this case and, as such, according to him, by non-production of the aforesaid material witnesses, particularly the Investigating Officer and the chemical examiner and also non-production of the alamats of the case before the trial Court, an adverse presumption ought to have been drawn against the prosecution case as the defence was seriously prejudiced for their non-production in court. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the appellant has relied on some decisions—one in the case of Nazir Ahmed & ors. Vs. State reported in 1985 BCR 279 and another in the case of Ismail Munshi Vs. State, 33 DLR 5 and another in the case of ARM Reza and others Vs. State reported in 9 DLR 594 and about non-production of alamats, he has relied on a decision in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Paran Chandra Baroi reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 225. 

 12. Mr. Enamul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the State, on the other hand, submitted the in view of section 134 of the Evidence Act, it was the quality and not the quantity of witnesses which was to be looked into and even conviction could be maintained on the basis of a single reliable and truthful solitary witness. As regards non-examination of the Investigating Officer, his submission was that unless it was shown that for such non-production of the Investigating Officer the defence was prejudiced, there should not be any adverse presumption drawn against the prosecution case and in this connection he relied on a decision in the case of Bhagaban Chandra Chakma Vs. State reported in 1987 BLD 351 = 38 DLR 374 and as regards non-production of some other witnesses, he submitted that if it was found that apart from those witnesses, the prosecution was able to prove its case beyond all reasonable doubt by the witness already produced then, non-production of any other witness or witnesses would not affect the merit of the prosecution case. In this connection, he relied on a decision in the case of Md. Abdul Karim Mondal Vs. Fazlul Bari and others reported in 33 DLR 397.
